It's 15 July 2032, at the BVG headquarters. Andrei is sitting in front of two people: Mrs Demir, head of the digital department, and Mr Kowalczyk, from HR.
Mr Ionescu, we're glad you've come. First tell us something about yourself.
Gladly. I'm from Sibiu, Romania, and I've been living in Berlin for four years. I did my master's in computer science at the TU, specialising in mobile apps.
In your cover letter you mention an app for blind people. Can you explain how it works?
It uses voice messages to show where the nearest stop is and when the bus is coming. The most important thing was that we tested it together with blind people, not just in the office.
What would you call your greatest weakness?
I'm sometimes impatient when decisions take a long time. I'm working on it. My neighbour says I should learn from tram drivers: they wait till everyone has got on, too.
Your neighbour sounds like a wise man. Do you have any questions for us?
Yes, I do. Could you tell me what the induction period looks like? And I'd like to know whether I'd work directly with the passenger associations.
The induction lasts three months. And yes, you'd test with passengers every week. With real passengers, at real stops.
May I also ask when you'll decide?
We'll get in touch by the end of the week. Thank you, Mr Ionescu.

1. Indirect questions with a question word
A direct question becomes indirect after an introductory phrase. The question word stays, and the verb goes to the END:
Könnten Sie mir sagen, wann die Probezeit endet?
Darf ich fragen, wie groß das Team ist?
Wissen Sie, wo der Raum 204 ist?
Common mistake: “Können Sie mir sagen, wann endet die Probezeit?” ✗. In an indirect question the verb comes at the end: “…, wann die Probezeit endet?” ✓
When the direct question starts with the verb (a yes/no answer), in the indirect one you use “ob” (= whether, if):
Ich wüsste gern, ob Homeoffice möglich ist.
Ich weiß nicht, ob ich die Stelle bekomme.

Don't confuse “ob” with “wenn”! “wenn” = if (condition) / when. “ob” = whether, if (question, uncertainty). English uses “if” for both, German doesn't: “Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt” — never “wenn” here.
How you can start your answer
Ich komme aus … und habe … studiert. Zurzeit …
Warum haben Sie sich bei uns beworben?
Ich bin manchmal …, aber ich arbeite daran, indem …
Wo sehen Sie sich in fünf Jahren?
For “weakness”, say something real but not serious, and show how you're working on it. “Ich bin Perfektionist” is a cliché every interviewer has heard a thousand times.
Darf ich fragen, mit wie vielen Kollegen ich zusammenarbeiten würde?
Könnten Sie mir sagen, wann Sie sich entscheiden?
About salary: it's usually asked at the second interview or if you're asked. If you're asked: “Meine Gehaltsvorstellung liegt bei … Euro brutto im Jahr.”
Do you know where room 204 is?
I don't know whether I'll get the job.
My greatest strength is that I'm reliable.
We'll get in touch by Friday.

On the morning of the fifteenth of July, Andrei woke up at six, although the interview wasn't till ten. He had the day off, for the first time in months: Jakob had taken over the bakery, remarking that a teacher on summer holiday could bake rolls just as well as a computer scientist. Andrei showered, shaved twice, put on the white shirt Lena had ironed and then the navy-blue suit he had bought for his graduation ceremony at the TU. He looked in the mirror and hardly recognised himself. “You look like an insurance salesman,” said Lena, when she brought him a coffee. And then she gave him a kiss and said: “A very handsome insurance salesman.”

Down in the courtyard Ludwig was waiting for him, in his armchair, which on warm days he had carried out under the chestnut tree. The evening before he had asked him all the questions an HR manager might ask and a few that only a former tram driver would ask: “What do you do if a passenger swears at you? What do you do if the power goes off at two in the morning? What do you do if a child wants to press the bell?” Andrei had answered them all. Now Ludwig just said: “Don't forget to breathe. And remember: they want you too. Otherwise they wouldn't have invited you.”

Andrei took the underground, not the tram, because he didn't want to risk being late. On the crowded U2 he stood among tourists with maps and workers with coffee cups and went over all his answers in his head. Tell us about yourself. Why us. Strengths, weaknesses. He realised he was thinking of the answers in Romanian and then translating them into German, and he got annoyed. Then he remembered something Mara had told him before her own B1 exam: when you start dreaming in German, you've won. Last night he had dreamt of trams. In German. That, he thought, would have to be enough.

The BVG headquarters was on Holzmarktstraße, on the bank of the Spree, a big modern glass building. Andrei arrived twenty minutes early. He sat down in the entrance hall, waited and tried to breathe calmly, as Ludwig had told him. On the wall opposite hung big photos from the history of the Berlin tram: horse-drawn trams from 1865, yellow carriages from the twenties, rubble and rails from 1945. And then, right at the end of the row, a photo that took Andrei's breath away.

It was a photo from October 2027. An old Tatra tram, number 5218, red and beige, on the route through Prenzlauer Berg. And in the driver's cab, with an old BVB cap on his head and a grin from ear to ear, sat Ludwig. Underneath, a little plaque said: “Ludwig Brandt, 41 years of service, on his last run on the number 46. Photo: Kurt Wolff, Tram Museum.” Andrei stood up and looked at the photo for a long time. He had heard the story of this run a hundred times. He hadn't known it was hanging here on the wall.

The interview lasted an hour. Mrs Demir was a slim woman who spoke fast, with short black hair, and typed something into her laptop after every answer. Mr Kowalczyk was older, calmer and smiled a lot. Andrei talked about his studies, about the app for blind people, about the test runs in Sibiu with Mr Dobre, who had been blind from birth and found every mistake in the app straight away. He talked about his impatience. And when Mrs Demir asked him why he wanted to work at the BVG in particular, he told her, without thinking about it for long, about the photo in the entrance hall.

The man in the last photo is my neighbour. He lives below me. Today he doesn't take the tram any more, not even as a passenger, because he doesn't know at which stops he can get on with his knee. The app doesn't tell him. I'd like to know whether you would let me change that.

Mrs Demir stopped typing. Mr Kowalczyk looked at her and raised his eyebrows. Then Mrs Demir stood up, went to the door and called into the corridor: “Kurt? Have you got a moment?” And in came a man of about sixty, with a grey moustache and an old camera round his neck, who introduced himself as Kurt Wolff, head of the Tram Museum and, as he added, “forty-seven years ago apprentice to a certain Ludwig Brandt”.

You live above Ludwig? Then you know what it's like. In my first year he taught me that a tram doesn't run for the driver, but for the passenger who gets on most slowly. If you've understood that, young man, then you're in the right place.

Andrei didn't know what to say. Kurt Wolff winked at him and told him, as if they were alone in a pub and not at a job interview, about his first day in 1985: how Ludwig had made him wait at the terminus in Pankow, a whole hour, in the snow, just so that he would learn that passengers have to wait too and that you must never forget that. “I hated him for it,” said Wolff. “For three weeks. Then I understood that he had taught me the most important thing you can learn in this job. And you, Mr Ionescu, seem to have learned it already. Without the snow.”

Mrs Demir sat down again and said with a little smile: “Mr Ionescu, I have to tell you that we actually only wanted to get in touch with you at the end of the week. We have two more candidates. Both of them have more professional experience than you.” Andrei nodded. He had expected that. “But,” Mrs Demir went on, “neither of them explained to us who they actually want to build this app for. You did. Could you tell me whether you can start on the first of September?”

Andrei had to clear his throat before he could answer. “Yes,” he said. “Yes, of course. May I ask whether…” He stopped. He had prepared so many questions, about the induction, the team, further training, and now he couldn't think of a single one. Mr Kowalczyk laughed kindly. “Ask anything you like when you sign the contract,” he said. “We'll send it to you next week. And, Mr Ionescu: bring your neighbour along to the first test run. We need someone who'll tell us honestly what's wrong with our app.”

When Andrei got back to Kastanienallee at half past twelve, Ludwig was still sitting under the chestnut tree in the courtyard, as if he hadn't moved since the morning. Lena was at the window on the first floor, Mara at the window on the fourth floor, Kuba and Ola at the window on the second floor. The whole house was waiting. Andrei said nothing. He went over to Ludwig, took out of his bag a little package that Kurt Wolff had given him as he left and put it on Ludwig's knees. Inside was an old brass bell from a Tatra tram, polished, with a note: “For Ludwig. So you can press it one more time. Kurt.”

Ludwig looked at the bell. Then he looked at Andrei. And then he pressed it, once, loud and clear, like sixty years ago, when a tram driver let a little boy on the number 46 do it. The sound rang through the whole courtyard, up to the fourth floor, and applause came from every window. “The first of September,” Andrei said at last. “I start on the first of September.” Ludwig pressed the bell again. And again. And Lena, up at the window, was crying and laughing at the same time and shouting: “Grandpa, stop, the neighbours!” But the neighbours, you could see, didn't mind at all.

In the evening they celebrated at the café “Bei Ingrid”, all together, at two tables pushed together. In honour of the day Jakob had baked a cake that hadn't quite worked, but everyone bravely ate it. Ludwig had brought the brass bell and put it next to the till. “From today,” he declared solemnly, “every child who orders a hot chocolate here may ring it once.” Lena rolled her eyes. But the next morning, when the first little boy came into the café with his mother and carefully pressed the bell, she smiled. And she wrote in chalk on the board by the door: “Ringing allowed.”
